statements.statement: Raw TCP: "No HTTP framing or WebSocket handshakes are needed." The connection is persistent and commands can be sent one after another. The Hercules walkthrough says to click Send "or press Enter with `<CR><LF>` enabled".
The server processes each command "on LightAct's main thread" and replies immediately.

Single requests only: "Batch/array execution is currently deferred." Do not send JSON-RPC batch arrays.

Time: floating point seconds (`float`) relative to the beginning of the timeline.
Distances: meters, `[x, y, z]`.
Angles: degrees, `[pan, tilt, roll]`.
Colors: normalized RGBA array `[r, g, b, a]`, each component `0.0` to `1.0`.

statements.statement: Supported 3D formats: **.fbx** and **.obj**, and "to an extent" .dae.
FBX is the preferred format and has the best support.
To apply content to a 3D model it must be properly UV mapped and its normals must face the correct way.
Render mode: default is **Shaded** (best for general visualisation in the Viewport).
If the 3D model is a Source for a projector, always use **Unshaded** render mode, otherwise the content will not look as intended.
Use as much of the UV map as possible. Wasted UV space costs VRAM.
In most cases the UV map should have no overlapping areas. In Blender, **Smart UV Project** usually achieves this.
Exception: surfaces that always show the same content (example given: wheels of a car) may overlap.
Check the UV map in Blender by applying a grid texture to the model.

statements.statement: Options live in the properties menu of the **Assets** window.
**FileWatcher**: monitors the asset repository. If enabled, a file copied into the repository is ingested the moment it lands.
Disable FileWatcher if you want manual control over when assets are ingested.
**Get data**: reads the Asset and makes it ready to play. LightAct must Get the Data of an Asset before it can play it.
Versioning works for all asset types.
To enable it, add `_versionName` to the end of the Asset's filename.
Examples given: `_v1`, `_v2`, `_v3`; `_YYMMDD` (or any 6 numbers); `_YYMMDDa`, `_YYMMDDb`, `_YYMMDDc`.
Pick one naming method and stick to it. Then, when a new version of an Asset is imported, LightAct automatically uses it.
Supported audio: **.mp3** and **.wav**.
Stereo only "at the moment".
Notch blocks: **.dfxdll** file extension. Both Notch 0.9xxx and 1.0 and above are supported.
TouchDesigner components: **.tox** files.
Details are in the real-time content playback section (Notch page and TouchDesigner page), not here.
Video files, single images and image sequences are all treated as a **Video asset** and used in more or less the same way.
Containers: **.mp4** and **.mov**. The container does not determine the codec (a .mov can hold H.264, NotchLC or HAP).
LightAct only decodes. It cannot encode.
Codecs decoded on the CPU: **H.264**.
Codecs decoded on the GPU: **NotchLC**, **HAP**, **HAPa**, **HAPQ**. Much better performance (maximum resolution at a given framerate), much larger files.
For the highest number of concurrent videos, HAP is usually recommended.
Codecs not in the table may play if they are in a supported container, but they are not fully supported and performance may be limited.
Performance benchmarks exist only for HAP and NotchLC. LightAct does not optimise for or benchmark ProRes, H.264 or other codecs.
Images: **.png**, **.jpg**, **.tga**, **.tiff**. For best performance .png or .tiff is recommended.
A single image file is treated as a video file with one frame.
All frames must have the same file extension. No mixing png and jpg.

statements.statement: Each DMX controllable property takes one channel in the Timeline's footprint, set by the Channel offset column.
Play state: one channel. Each play state has a range of values (Timeline state channel value ranges). Ranges must not overlap.
Cues: every Cue (Section or Marker) has three Cue numbers, X, Y and Z. Each Timeline has 3 DMX channels for Cue triggering. A Cue fires when those 3 channel values match its CueX, CueY and CueZ.

Every layer has **Universe** and **Channel** properties in the **DMX** variable group. Default is -1, meaning not DMX controlled.
Map a layer by dragging from a channel to the layer. This sets Universe and Channel.

All Stock Layer templates have DMX footprints already set up.
Per variable (right-click menu): **Include in DMX In** checkbox decides if it is in the footprint. Bit depth can be 8, 16, 24 or 32 bit.
Mapping, Device and Asset variables are controlled through Index Manager.
DMX flag: disable it to stop DMX setting that variable temporarily. It turns green while DMX is setting the variable.
**Remap value** unchecked: the variable gets the raw DMX channel value. Checked: value is scaled between the variable's Min and Max. Example: Min 0, Max 1000, DMX 255 gives 1000, DMX 0 gives 0.

Global variables are set up for DMX the same way as Layer variables.

Timelines, Sections and Layers all have Fade in and Fade out, but they behave differently.

Timeline fade in/out does not act at the start or end of the Timeline. It applies when the Timeline switches play modes. Example: fade in 3 seconds, timeline stopped, pressing play fades content in over 3 seconds wherever the playhead is.
Apply fade to Pause (Timeline): checked means the fade applies when switching between any play state and Pause or Stop. Unchecked means only between any play state and Stop.
Section Fade in/out applies to all layers at the beginning and end of the section.
Layer Fade in/out applies to that layer only.
Layer fades and Section fades multiply with each other.
Cross-fade applies when jumping from one part of the timeline to another. Set on Timeline, Section or Layer.
The Timeline's Cross-fade applies to sections and layers only where their Cross-fade is set to Inherit.
Inherit: a Section inherits from the Timeline, a Layer inherits from its Section.

Action flow decides which nodes execute. It is set by Lifeline connections, and every Lifeline starts at a Lifeline generator node.
Default generators: Tick, On Begin, On End.
Other generators: many nodes have a "New message" lifeline output. They are meant for receiving network messages together with receiving Device nodes.
Blinking connection lines show that a layer is active.
Lifeline: lime, square pins. One lifeline output connects to only one lifeline input. One lifeline input can take several lifeline outputs. This is the reverse of most other connection types.
Two chain types: lifeline chain (nodes joined by lifeline) and sub-chain (nodes joined by other connection types). A sub-chain only executes if it is connected to the lifeline chain.
Connection colour shows the data type. Examples: dark red is float, light blue is string.
Only pins of the same colour connect, and only output to input.
A connection is active only while the Playhead is on the layer and the connection leads back to a lifeline generator.

With Tick as generator: (1) execute the node connected to Tick, (2) to do so, first execute all sub-chains connected to that node, (3) move to the next node on the lifeline, (4) finish when all connected nodes are done.
Nodes not connected are not executed.
The lifeline can be split with conditional nodes (the If node, with a boolean Input) or delayed.
Special variable type: CV Mat, also called CV. All Computer Vision nodes take CV in and give CV out.
Convert nodes (Search menu, Utilities -> General, "Convert"): Texture to CV (drag from a Texture output pin) and CV to Texture (drag from a CV output pin). A typical CV workflow uses both.
Keep the resolution of CV streams low to save system resources.
Compares current and previous frame. Output is a CV image in HSV: H is movement direction, V is velocity.

Input pins: CV input; Scales number (higher is more detail, lower it if slow); Scales step (a ratio); Median filter size (higher is blurrier, raise for fast objects); Threshold magnitude (if the max magnitude in the image is below it, output is black); Dynamic magnitude (off: per-pixel magnitude divided by the Normalize magnitude parameter and stored in V. On: max magnitude maps to 255, min to 0, linear in between); Dynamic Flow (on: also uses results from the previous detection).
Output pins: Output; Max magnitude (max velocity of detected parts, not normalised).
For small fast objects, Scales number and Scales step can be reduced.
Finds groups of connected pixels in a CV input.

Input pins: Input (CV Mat with 1, 3 or 4 channels); Filter by threshold (uses Min threshold and Max threshold); Filter by area (uses Min area and Max area); Min distance (blobs closer than this are merged); Max track count (max blobs in the output).
Output pin: Relative X, Y, area. Formatted as x position/image width, y position/image height, blob area/image area.
Separates foreground from background.

Input pins: Input (CV Mat, 1, 3 or 4 channels); History (number of frames used to build the background image); Learn rate (below 0: chosen automatically. Equal to 0 or above 1: background is not updated. Exactly 1: background always updates with the last input); Threshold variance; Detect Shadows (shadows shown grey).
Output pins: Output (foreground white, background black, shadows grey); Background (the background image).
Merges several CV Mats into one, for example overlapping cameras.
Input pins: Resolution (width and height of the output CV Mat); Inputs (one pin per CV stream). Output pin: Output.

Subtracts two CV inputs into one output that takes the resolution of the first input. A node property lets it output the absolute value.

Markerless tracking with depth cameras installed on a ceiling. Works in dark or bright spaces, indoors and outdoors.
Two tracking modes: **Simulation** and **LightTrack live**.

**Simulation**: tracks *People* objects in the Viewport. No special hardware. Works with the free LightAct license. Steps: add a LightTrack sensor and a LightTrack system to the Viewport. In the *LightTrack system* properties under *Sources*, double click the sensors to add them. Move the *LightTrack sensor* above a *People* object. Click **Start** in the *LightTrack system* properties.

**LightTrack live**: tracks physical people. Needs a paid LightAct license and hardware. Steps: add an OAK receiver node in the *Devices* window. Add a LightTrack sensor in the *Viewport* and choose the *OAK camera* as source. Add a LightTrack system and choose the *LightTrack sensor* as source. Click **Start** in the LightTrack system properties.
Use the **Get LightTrack data** node in a Layer Layout to read the tracking data.
**LightTrack system**: viewport object that aggregates data from sensors. Drag from the *Side bar* to the *Viewport*.
**LightTrack sensor**: viewport object that reads data from a device such as an OAK camera. Place it to mimic the physical space. Properties include the source device and settings such as FOV.

Hardware: SICK Visionary-T Mini camera, Visionary mounting kit (recommended), 24V DC power supply, power cable M12 8-pin A-coded (10 m recommended), Ethernet cable M12 8-pin X-coded to RJ45, 1 Gbit or faster switch, dedicated NIC (recommended).
Set a static IP on the computer's network adapter. Sharing the network with internet traffic is supported but not recommended.
Camera IPs: in **SICK AppManager**, click **Search**, select a camera, assign a static IP, repeat. Example: 10.10.10.10, 10.10.10.11, 10.10.10.12.
Verify in LightAct: **Devices** window, add **SICK Visionary Camera Receiver**, select camera, click **Receive**, check the depth stream is visible.

Mounting: same distance to the surface, perpendicular to the surface, same orientation, firm (no vibration), minimum 20% overlap between cameras, avoid reflective surfaces. Mount one by one and check coverage. Overlap is required for multi-camera tracking.
Measure and write down: camera height from lens to floor, and horizontal distance between cameras. Both are needed for LightTrack setup.
Receivers: in **Devices**, add one **SICK Visionary Camera Receiver** per camera, rename each, click **Receive**.

Depth filtering, in **Device Settings**: reduce **Max depth** until the floor is completely black (value close to the measured height), then raise **Min depth** to fine-tune. Tracked objects should look as white as possible in the stream, unwanted objects as black as possible.
Sensors: drag one **LightTrack Sensor** per camera into the viewport and rename. Position: Y = measured height, X = horizontal distance between cameras, Z = 0. First camera at X = 0.
For each sensor: Properties, Source, select its SICK Visionary Camera Receiver. Set HFOV = 70° for all sensors.
System: add a **LightTrack System**, add all sensors under **Sources**, under **Tracking** select **LightTrack**, click **Start**.
Threshold: select the receiver node, hold CTRL, click the darkest area you want to track, use that value as Threshold.
Blob tracking: under **Input**, adjust Min diameter, Max diameter and Min distance. Objects closer than the minimum distance are merged.
Overlap alignment: place an object in the overlap area and adjust **Inward offset** until blobs from both cameras align.

Command: `-log`; Effect: Extensive logging. The Log Window shows extended messages for Iris cameras, down-sampling, up-sampling and so on.
Command: `-developer`; Effect: Shows developer information such as object IDs, down-sampled resolutions and more.

Command: `-secondary`; Effect: Gives the machine a Secondary role in LightNet.
Command: `-lightnet`; Effect: Sets the LightNet checkbox to ON.
Command: `-project "<filepath>"`; Effect: Opens the given project on launch.
Command: `-window "<poz.x> <poz.y>"`; Effect: Sets the position of the program window on launch.
Command: `-window "<poz.x> <poz.y> <size.x> <size.y>"`; Effect: Sets the position and size of the program window on launch.
Command: `-nic "<ip> <port>"`; Effect: Sets the default NIC and data port for the application. If the NIC is not valid, a default NIC is set.

Custom launch arguments: any `-key "value"` pair. The string after the dash is the key, the string in quotation marks is the value. Read it in a layout with the **Get Launch Argument** node.

`layout-nodes.md` lists 14 categories, in this order.
Tick: Triggered every frame when layer is active. Default outputs: Lifeline.
On Begin: Triggered once when layer is started. Default outputs: Lifeline.
On End: Triggered once when layer is ended. Default outputs: Lifeline.
Sequence: Splits lifeline impulse. Default inputs: Lifeline. Default outputs: Lifeline. Search keywords: fork.
On shutdown: Triggered once when application is shutting down. Default outputs: Lifeline. Search keywords: close exit.
Key up/down: Triggers event on key press. Default outputs: Lifeline. Search keywords: keypress, key press.
Switch case: Classic switch-case checker. Default inputs: Lifeline. Default outputs: Lifeline. Supported types: Integer, Float, String, Vec2, Vec3, Timecode.
Run once: Forwards tick until reset. Default inputs: Lifeline. Default outputs: Lifeline.
Run every: Runs on a set interval. Default inputs: Float. Default outputs: Lifeline.
Delayed tick: Delays tick trigger. Default inputs: Lifeline, Integer. Default outputs: Lifeline.
Cycle: Cycles between outputs. Default inputs: Lifeline. Default outputs: Lifeline.
For loop: Repeats until a condition is false. Default inputs: Integer, Lifeline. Default outputs: Integer, Lifeline.
Foreach: Executes for each element in an array. Default inputs: Integer, Lifeline. Default outputs: Integer, Lifeline. Search keywords: loop.
Run on marker: Runs when selected marker is reached. Default outputs: Lifeline.

Go to marker: Moves the playhead to the selected marker. Looping is possible if "Go to next" or "Go to previous" is selected. Default inputs: Lifeline, Integer, LA Object. Default outputs: Lifeline. Search keywords: jump.
Go to section: Jumps to specified section. Default inputs: Lifeline, LA Object, Integer. Default outputs: Lifeline. Search keywords: jump.
Go to landmark: Jumps to next or previous timeline landmark. Default inputs: Lifeline. Default outputs: Lifeline.
Set layer state, Deprecated: Sets layer state. Default inputs: Lifeline, Boolean. Default outputs: Lifeline.
Get device status, Deprecated, use Get data: Returns device status information. Default inputs: Device. Default outputs: Boolean.
Set device status: Sets device status information. Default inputs: Lifeline, Device, Boolean. Default outputs: Lifeline. Not marked deprecated.

Send OSC node inputs: **Device** (the OSC Sender) and **Address** (string).
Bundle messages: several values to the same address using one OSC Sender device. Create several **Send OSC** nodes, chain them through their **Lifeline** input/output, and tick **Send as bundle**.
The receiver reads individual values from the bundle with the **Index** input of a **Read OSC** node.

statements.statement: Receiving, Devices window: insert a **MIDI receiver** node, select a *Stream* source, tick **Receive**.
Incoming MIDI Timecode is shown at the bottom of the node's Data section.
MTC must be in **MTC Short Message** format or LightAct cannot parse it.
The MIDI Receiver node's properties include a **Timecode offset**, applied to everything that uses this timecode afterwards.
Receiving, Layouts window: place a **Read MIDI** node and select the MIDI receiver device. Right-click an output pin and choose **Watch** to see values.

Controlling Layers with MIDI: in the **MIDI In** window click **Regenerate**. Every layer variable with its MIDI flag enabled gets a unique MIDI Control and Value combination. When that MIDI message arrives, the variable is set.
Sending, Devices window: place a **MIDI Sender** node, choose *Stream* parameters such as *Timecode rate* and Stream output, tick **Send**.
Sending, Layouts window: place a **Send Mtc** node and select the MIDI sender device as its input.
Two steps: **Output Maps** (map Viewport object content onto Physical outputs), then **Output management** (correct framerates, sync, EDIDs).

*Output Maps* window has 3 areas: **Viewport objects** (those selected in Properties on the right), **Virtual outputs** (mapped or not yet mapped), **Physical outputs** (all detected outputs, on all machines in a multi-machine setup).
Order: 1. Create Virtual outputs. 2. Map objects to Virtual outputs, then Virtual outputs to Physical outputs. 3. Enable the Virtual outputs.

Create a Virtual output: right click a Physical output and pick **Create matching output** (same resolution) or **Create and map matching output** (same resolution, also mapped). Double click a Physical output also creates a matching Virtual output. Right click in the *Outputs* area to create one at other resolutions.
Mapping Viewport objects to Virtual outputs works the same as in Canvas Maps. A Mapping layout can also be created in Output Maps.

Map Virtual to Physical: drag from the Virtual output's Properties icon to a Physical output. **Shift + drag** maps and enables. Or left click the Properties icon (top right of each Virtual output) and use its Mapping section.
Enable: Properties icon, then Enable. Enabling creates a new full screen window that covers that output entirely.
Shortcut: dragging creates a Virtual output with the same resolution as the Source area and maps it to that Physical output. Shift-dragging also enables it.
Recommendations: understand vsync handling, use fixed EDIDs wherever possible, use Mosaic wherever possible.

Vsync rules: with no outputs enabled, LightAct is vertically synced to its UI display. As soon as one output is enabled, it releases vsync from the UI display and enables vsync to the output display. Automatic.
Manual vsync: enable **Remote support** in the *General* tab of *Preferences*, then set the **Vertical sync** dropdown in the *General* tab of *Project settings*.

Fixed EDID means loading the EDID from a file, so the OS always assumes the display is attached. Protects against hot plug events and EDID loss through switchers and extenders. Two ways: in LightAct, or in NVIDIA Control Panel.

Multiple outputs on one machine: strongly recommended to combine them into an Nvidia Mosaic (presented to the OS as a single logical GPU). Keep the UI display separate and put all output displays in the Mosaic.
Mosaic can currently only be enabled from NVIDIA Control Panel.
Without Mosaic: all outputs need the same refresh rate, and should be synced with a Quadro Sync card (Sync Expansion Module).
Before starting: remove the Windows user password or set automatic login, so the machine can be entered after a crash or bluescreen during setup.
Only displays with the same resolution and framerate can be combined.
NVIDIA Control Panel, *Workstation*, **Set up Mosaic**, **Create new configuration**.

If GPUs are not sync-capable (see *Sync capability* icon), enable V-Sync: *3D Settings*, **Manage 3D Settings**, **Global Settings** tab, *Global presets* set to **Base profile**, *Vertical sync* **On**, **Apply**.
Multi-projector or stereoscopic 3D installations must use Mosaic with sync-capable GPUs.
*Select topology*: **Number of displays**, **Topology**, **Orientation of displays**, **Configuration name**.
Limits (NVIDIA): all displays need at least one display timing in common. Each display must be greater than 800x600. Total Mosaic resolution must not exceed 16,384 pixels horizontally or vertically.
*Select displays*: choose displays, **Refresh rate**, **Resolution per display**. *Arrange displays*: set order (note it down for mapping in LightAct), then **Apply**.
Applications using the NVIDIA driver may need to be closed (click **Continue**). Displays may flash. Applying can take more than 30 seconds.
*Apply Changes* pop up gives about 20 seconds to click **Yes**. If missed, NVIDIA Control Panel may misbehave: close it, reopen, restart the process.
Optional last step: *Adjust overlap and bezel correction*. Edge overlap needs sync-capable GPUs.
NVIDIA Control Panel, *Workstation*, **Set Up Mosaic**. **Modify** reopens the setup window. **Disable**, then **Disable** again in the pop up.
Mosaic driver issues: remove NVIDIA drivers, shut down, check all monitor cables, boot, reinstall drivers.

BSOD or freeze during Mosaic: caused by changing the setup while in Mosaic mode (adding or removing monitors), total resolution above 16,384 pixels in either direction, or exceeding PCIe bus data limits.

BSOD while Mosaic was Primary Display: usually leaves Windows login unreachable if the password was not removed. Boot from the Windows Recovery USB dongle shipped with the reActor server, **Troubleshoot**, **Advanced options**, **Startup Settings**, **Restart**, press **4** or **F4** for Safe Mode, uninstall all NVIDIA drivers, remove password or set autologin, reboot, reinstall drivers.
Only some Mosaic displays show content: check Vertical Sync is On in NVIDIA Control Panel, all monitors connected and active, disable and re-create the Mosaic, then treat as a driver issue.
Flickering black bars on outputs: Nvidia driver bug, not tearing. Mitigate by enabling triple buffering in NVidia settings.
Nvidia-smi.exe error: likely a GPU driver issue. No known workaround other than reinstalling all graphics drivers.
Applies only to LightAct servers, not multi-GPU systems in general.
LightAct has no native "select GPU" feature.

Typical reActor multi-GPU configuration: 1 GPU for GUI output, 2 GPUs for Video Outputs. By default this does not make full use of the output GPUs. Extra steps are needed (Mosaic, Primary Display, Workflow).

statements.statement: LightNet: create **LightNetProjects** on the D: (storage) drive, share with Everyone Read/Write, then set it in Edit > Preferences > Network > LightNet Projects folder path.

Throttling test: enable **Remote support mode** in Preferences (this unlocks **Vertical sync** in Project settings). Untick **Vertical sync** and **Force Project framerate**. Expect well over 1000 FPS and, more important, a steady figure. Dips every few seconds mean the GPU is being throttled.

Smoothness test: re-enable both checkboxes. In **Output Maps** double-click a detected Physical output to make a virtual output of the same resolution. Enable a content override (**Strobe**, **Traveling gradient** or **Traveling lines**) and the output. Motion must be completely smooth.
Multiple displays must be combined into a Mosaic to be completely smooth.
Uses the **Video Playback Template project**. Needs LightAct 4.11.0-89 or newer, Advanced Renamer, MediaInfo.
Example rig: 4 x 4K outputs, 1 GUI plus 3 in Mosaic (11520x2160). 60Hz for 30/60 fps videos, 50Hz for 25/50 fps.

Test videos: HAP with chunks = number of CPU cores, or NotchLC at Best quality. Constant bitrate. Copies named `VideoFileName_1`, `VideoFileName_2`, and so on, because each Play video node must play a unique file. LightAct can supply its reference test file.
Close all other apps, including NVIDIA Control Panel. Keep only the Performance window (and Timeline editor) open. Main window fullscreen (F11).

The **Loading thumbnails** layer waits, then the **Video layer** starts a new Play video node every 1 to 2 seconds. Both have a `Delay`. Marker 1 logs "Test started", Marker 2 logs "Test concluded". Output runs the **Traveling Lines** override.
Assign each video variable of the Video layer to a different file, save, reopen the project.
Result: the highest count with no continuous **Missed frames** in the Performance window (initial ones are fine) and smooth Traveling Lines.
Symptoms: outputs out of sync, motion not smooth, large periodic graph spikes. One unstable server can upset the whole system.

Simplify: one GUI display and one output display per server. Output display on Genlock or Framelock, GUI display not synced. Not needed if Primary has no output display. Same refresh rate everywhere, equal to project framerate. Dedicated switch with only LightAct machines.
Close remote desktop tools (VNC Viewer, TeamViewer, AnyDesk), browsers, GPU monitoring tools, NVIDIA Control Panel. Apps that interact with desktop rendering can affect sync.
Test: establish cluster, enable outputs in Output Maps with Content override **Strobe**, begin LightSync session. Then reconnect equipment step by step.
Multiple outputs should be one NVIDIA Mosaic display.
For support: a video of all outputs with the Output Maps **Render overlay** on (LightAct 4.16.0 or newer), a screenshot of NVIDIA Control Panel > View System Topology, and a Package for support.
Direct DP to DP is recommended. Not all converters work. Tested: StarTech **DP2HDMI2** and **DP2HDMI4KS**.
Steps: Projection study (usually before projectors are connected), then Projection mapping.
*2D projection Mapping*: flat or curved surfaces such as screens and walls.
*3D Projection Mapping*: complex 3D objects. Needs an accurate 3D model of the projection object. Content is usually rendered onto that 3D model. May use Iris.
In a multi-server setup, *Projection Study* runs only on the *Primary* machine.
Set the Render mode of the projection object to *Unshaded* for best results.
Setup: place objects in the *Viewport*, add projectors and set their **Properties**, map the objects to the projectors.
Open with **Tools**, **Projection Study**. Select projectors and objects to analyse, choose a mode in the *Setup* section, click **Enable**.

Four modes: **Projected content** (how the projection will look), **Shadow analysis** (areas getting no light), **Illuminance** (adjustable lux scale, for projector count and lumen output), **Pixel size** (pixel grid on objects, shows pixel stretching).
When enabled, a tag appears at the upper left of the *Viewport* and only the chosen objects and projectors are shown.
Blending (AutoBlend) results can be viewed in *Projected content* and *Illuminance* modes.
In 2D projection mapping you usually do not use Projector viewport objects at all. All warping and blending is done in the Output Maps window.

Initial calculations: from object size, required brightness and viewing distance, determine projector count, resolution, lens properties and overlap (in pixels or percent). Then calculate the overall content resolution.

Project setup (one option): create a Video screen with the correct physical size and resolution and render test content to it. In **Output Maps** create one *Virtual output* per projector. **Create subareas** in the *Video screen* matching projector resolution and snap them to the screen edges. **Map the subareas** to the Virtual outputs. Right click the destination subarea and select **Create layout**.
Mapping layout node chain: **Perspective warp** first (align corners), **Mesh warp** (fine tune), **Softedge** (blend projectors).
Warp one projector first, then the next relative to it. Blending is usually last.
For blending, switch to White Content override. Some users prefer red.
For colour mismatch between projectors use colour correction nodes in the Layout, for example *Texture Modify* or *Channel Multiply*.
The 3D model in the viewport must be a precise digital twin of the physical object. It needs proper UV mapping and correct normals to take a texture.

Steps: 1. Import and place precise 3D models (relative positions between objects must be accurate) and set them as the ***Sources*** of the projectors. 2. Calibrate projectors: with *Iris*, calibrate cameras first then all projectors automatically. Without Iris, use *3DCal* manually. 3. Blend with *AutoBlend*. 4. Fine-tune with warp, blend and colour correction nodes.

Two ways to set a projector's sources: the *Content section* in the projector's properties (double click a source or use the <> buttons), or drag from the objects to the projector. Mapped objects appear in the projector's thumbnail.
The object's render mode should be **Unshaded** for projection mapping.
3DCal matches a virtual projector's location, rotation and lens properties to the physical one, using at least 6 pairs of matching points on the virtual and physical object.
Point rules: not all on the same plane, non symmetrical, spread across the whole projected part of the object. Breaking the first two can look fine but place the projector wrongly.
*Reprojection* error should be kept below 1px.

First place the virtual projector roughly where the physical one is. Double click the projector, or right click and **Setup**, then the **3DCal** tab. Left preview is the view from the virtual projector, right preview is what the projector outputs.

Settings: **Output** (toggle whether points are sent to the output, disable after point selection to judge precision). **Viewport** (Render mode of the projected object). **Calibrate on change** (recalibrate on every new or moved point, otherwise only on the **Calibrate** button). **Snap to vertex** (clicks snap to the closest model vertex). **Adjust projection points** (moves projected points within the max delta range to lower reprojection error). **Preferences** (cursor colour, background colour, thickness). **Viewport** (toggle 3D helper spheres in the main Viewport, **Draw helper spheres**). **Fallbacks** (save, restore and compare calibration solutions).
Click **Store current orientation** first so you can revert if calibration moves the projector far away.
Virtual and physical points can be picked in any order. Virtual points are clicked on the left side.
Projected points are selected on the right side. The projector must already be mapped to an enabled physical output.
After the 6th pair the projector is calibrated and moved. Success means reprojection error below or close to 1.
Right click a point to delete it. Points can be moved with the mouse or arrow keys. Arrow keys move the cursor by 1px.
Automatically calculates blend masks for projectors or throwers.
Open with **F8** or **Tools**, **AutoBlend**. Select the projection objects and click **Blend**. Blend masks appear on the right.
All projected objects should have render mode *Unshaded*, otherwise blending might not be perfect.

Settings: **Blend on open** (recalculate when the project file opens). **Blend every frame** (recalculate every frame, only for moving projectors or objects). **Mute all AutoBlend nodes** (disables AutoBlend on the outputs).
**Run Autoblend** node triggers AutoBlend automatically.

**Blend with distance**: for projectors at different distances from the object. When enabled, distance is fully taken into account in the mask. Recommended practice is identical projectors at similar distances.

**Angle cutoff**: reduces pixel stretching on complex 3D objects. Applies the least blending to the projector hitting a face most perpendicularly and the most blending to the one with the sharpest angle. Gives fewer sharp edges between masks. It does not remove sharp mask edges caused by projector shadows.

Where masks are applied: double click a projector to open its Layout. The **AutoBlend** node outputs the blend mask into a **Texture Blend** node, which blends it with the content (the **Input** node). Masks can be adjusted further with nodes.
Iris is one or several *Power over Ethernet* machine vision cameras pre-calibrated by LightAct, used to calibrate projectors faster and more accurately.
Workflow: optional IrisVirtual, Setting up Iris Device Node, Adjusting Focus, Adding and Calibrating Iris Camera in Viewport, Calibrate Projectors.
Adjust the focus ring on the camera while clicking **Refresh the texture**. The **Circles and lines** override helps. Tighten the screw afterwards.
Estimates the number of Iris cameras needed, with location, orientation and lens type, before buying. Under development, features will likely change.

Process: add Iris cameras to the viewport and choose lenses, map the projection objects to them, open the **Iris** window, select the **Iris camera(s)** and all projectors, tick **IrisVirtual**, click **Calibrate**.
Projection objects must be properly UV mapped. Projection object resolution must be high enough: one pixel of the object should be the same size or smaller than a projected pixel.

Negative results: reprojection error above 1 px, or *"Insufficient number of points"*. Causes: camera does not see the entire projected area, or the area from one projector is too small in the camera view.
A positive result (below 1 px for all projectors) can still fail in reality. LightAct asks you to send the project file for review before deciding.

statements.statement: Create an *Iris device node* in the **Devices** window and select the physical camera from the dropdown. The camera must be powered and on the network to be listed.
**Mode** dropdown: *3DCal* or *Projector calibration*. Each mode stores its own *Exposure time*, *Gain* and *Gamma*. Changing a value saves it into the current mode.

**Exposure time [ms]**: higher is brighter. **Gain**: brightens bright areas more than dark ones, useful for *Projector calibration*. **Gamma**: lower is brighter, minimum 0.25, post process so click **Refresh texture** to see it. **Undistort**: keep checked at all times.

**Setup** button opens the *Iris* Setup window for masking. **Add polygon**, drag the handle to move, double click a line to add a point, right click a point to remove. Masked area shows red and is ignored for calibration. **Inverse mask** inverts it.

Settings for 3DCal (mode set to **3DCal**): object neither under nor over exposed. Recommended **Exposure** around 30000, **Gain** around 1, **Gamma** around 1. With no ambient light, set projectors to Edit color override for lighting.

Settings for Projector calibration (mode set to **Projector Calibration**): lit areas as white as possible, unlit as dark as possible. Tune with **Black and white override** enabled on a projector in the camera's view.
With a LightNet setup, when calibrating a projector connected to a Secondary machine, select the right Machine in the projector's Properties.

Black lines in incoming images (seen in the Iris folder in LightAct's Program Data folder during projector calibration): change network adapter settings. Network settings, Ethernet, Change adapter options, the adapter on the camera network, **Properties**, **Configure**, **Advanced** tab.

Vimba Viewer (part of the Allied Vision Vimba SDK) lists Iris cameras as Mako G-507B. Open a camera, click Freerun, All tab, Stream, Statistics. The marked fields should all be zero (which fields is only shown in a screenshot).
Open **Tools**, **Iris**. Select the cameras and projectors on the right.
**IrisVirtual**: uncheck for real projectors.
**Include Iris camera points**: includes points picked in the camera's 3DCal window. Leave checked in 99% of cases.
**Show advanced**: extra settings, rarely needed.
**Export calibration images**: saves every camera image from the calibration to *ProgramData\Lightact\Lightact4\iris*. Leave checked, support asks for these first.
**Adjust projection points**: adjusts projected points within *fix delta [px]* to lower reprojection error.
**Show in Explorer** opens that directory. **Calibrate** starts the process.

statements.statement: Layers live in Timelines. All content to play and all data to process passes through the layer system at some point.
Direct mappings: the layer renders straight onto a viewport object (for example a video screen).
context: Layers render to 3 types of mappings:

statements.statement: Canvases: a texture container that lets you map the texture, or parts of it, onto viewport objects.

statements.statement: Throwers: a virtual viewport object that "projects" content onto viewport objects.

statements.statement: Layers can also render to Device nodes. This is the usual way to send content out through NDI or video IO cards (Deltacast, Blackmagic).
All of the above destinations can also receive content through Set Texture nodes.
Timeline: where content (layers), events and actions are sequenced and composited. A project can have several independent timelines. A timeline holds Tracks, Sections, Layers and Markers.
Timeline group: one or more Timelines. Used to control syncing to external timecode sources and to control play states of the Timelines in it.
Track: a lane in a Timeline that holds one or more layers.

Layer: exists in a Timeline, has a beginning and an end (set by the Duration parameter). Does content playback and processing (video, image, image sequence, Notch block) or just logic. "Layers in LightAct are called Layer Templates."
Layouts: the node-based system. Found in Layers, in Mappings (Canvas Maps and Output Maps windows) and in Projectors.
Variable: a container for information (integer, float, color, texture and more). Layer variables exist within one layer. Global variables are accessible anywhere.
Section: part of a timeline. Often used as a cue.
Marker: a position on a Timeline.
Viewport: the visual preview of the real-world setup.
Video screen: virtual stand-in for a physical video screen.
Thrower: helper virtual object that maps content onto viewport objects using their position in the 3D scene.
3D model: usually imported as `.fbx` or `.obj` assets.
Primitive: a cube, plane, sphere or cone.
Null object: an empty object used as a container to group and move other objects.
Marker in Viewport: a 3D position in the Viewport window (separate from a Timeline marker).
Canvas: holds one texture of arbitrary resolution. Usually filled by Layers, then sent to viewport objects through the Canvas maps window.
Assets: external resources used by a project. Images, image sequences, video files, Notch blocks, TouchDesigner components, audio files, 3D models, Unreal Engine projects.
Video output: virtual stand-in for a physical output on the system's GPU.
DMX is DMX512. Art-Net and sACN are UDP-based protocols carrying DMX over Ethernet. Fixture means a DMX light fixture.
Windows are dockable. Drag them and drop on docking handles.
A Workspace is a saved window arrangement. Three predefined: Basic, Playback, Programming. Custom workspaces can be created.
A workspace is saved whenever the program closes or you switch to another workspace.

statements.statement: Do not save project files in Google Drive, Dropbox or similar synced folders. These services interfere with file access and can make LightAct crash or act oddly.
GUI black on launch: most likely an unsuitable GPU. Use a discrete Nvidia GPU.

Closes on launch (cache): delete certain files and folders in `C:\ProgramData\LightAct\LightAct4`. If that fails, uninstall completely including the Preferences, then reinstall. Contact support@lightact.com either way.
`"C:\Program Files\LightAct\LightAct4\LightAct4.exe" -omit "14"`
Adjust the path if installed elsewhere. The DirectShow Receiver node in the Devices window will then be unavailable.
Contact: support@lightact.com or Discord. First check you are on the latest version and that the docs do not cover the issue.
Always include: a Package for Support, a Bug Report, and the problem Assets if possible.

Package for Support (introduced in LightAct 4.13): zips the entire project folder except the Assets. Contains the project file, all log files, BugSplat crash dumps (if any) and other diagnostic information. Send any problem asset separately.
Bug report contents: Reproduction steps (short, clear), The result, Expected result, plus screenshots, screen recordings, and photos or videos of the outputs.
Unity has no native integration. Users run it on another machine, bring content in over NDI or live video input, and exchange data over UDP, OSC or TCP.

statements.statement: Usual route is the Notch layer template. The node inside it is **Play Notch Block**. Its input pins are the template's exposed Layer variables (see `docs/layers-and-layouts/stock-layer-templates/content-layer-templates/notch-layer-template.md`).
Node property **Unload on layer exit**: clears the block from VRAM on layer exit.
Needs a valid Notch license: **Playback**, or **Builder** at limited resolution. PLE is untested. Users report watermarked playback if the block was also exported with PLE.
Node Error with warning **Failed to load node contents** most likely means no suitable license.
Needs a discrete GPU, preferably Nvidia. GPU matters most for performance. Multi-GPU: contact LightAct first.
Copy .tox files into the **Assets/TouchDesigner** folder and they appear in LightAct. Play with the **Play TouchDesigner Component** node (asset dropdown).
Loading takes a minute or two after selecting the asset. The node then rebuilds itself with new input and output pins.
Needs TouchDesigner installed, with a Commercial license or above. Multi-GPU not supported.
Both apps run on one machine. LightAct controls the pace of Unreal's render cycle and passes runtime data such as Timecode.
Works with UE 4.27, or 5.1.1 and above. Not 5.0 or 5.1.0.
Required: the **LightAct** plugin (version must match the project's UE version), Epic's **Texture Share** and **nDisplay**. Creating the project from the nDisplay template enables the Epic ones.
Engine install: copy the **LightAct** folder to `<UEEngineVersion>\Engine\Plugins`. Available, not auto-enabled, in all projects on that version.
Project install: copy the **LightAct** folder into a **Plugins** folder in the project.
Enable under Settings > Plugins > **Installed** > **Enabled**, then restart Unreal Editor.
Three steps, detailed in the next three pages: LightAct Runtime actor, LightActTimeStep as Custom Time Step, LightActTimeCode as Timecode provider.

statements.statement: Lets LightAct drive Unreal's render cycle. The manual treats "Custom Timestep" and "Genlock" as the same thing.
Create a Blueprint Class asset with parent **LightActTimeStep**. Select it in UE Project Settings > **Custom TimeStep** dropdown.
Monitor: Window > Developer Tools > Genlock. Console: `stat fps`, `stat unit`.
Drag **LightAct Runtime** from Place Actors into the level. It passes performance and project data to LightAct by itself. No properties to set.
Create a Blueprint Class asset with parent **LightActTimeCode**. Select it in UE Project Settings > **Timecode Provider** dropdown.
Monitor: Window > Developer Tools > Timecode Provider.
**UnrealLink** is the LightAct window for the UE integration. Marked as under development.
UE Editor path (**UE4Editor.exe** or **UE5Editor.exe**) is set in **Preferences > UE**. It decides which UE version launches .uproject assets.

Sync: **Send timecode to UE**. **Genlock Unreal Engine** (off, every frame, every second, every third; usually Every frame). **Wait for UE texture** (sub-frame latency feature). If Unreal cannot keep up, lower LightAct's FPS in Project Settings.
Order: import Unreal asset, create .ndisplay file, generate launch command, launch nDisplay, optionally kill it.
Unreal asset = .exe of a packaged game or a .uproject. Drag it into LightAct's window. Assets show as radio buttons in UnrealLink. Select one.
The .ndisplay file needs at least one Thrower or Projector in the Viewport with its **nDisplay** checkbox on. Click **...** to pick or create the file, then **Generate config file**.
**Generate command** fills the command textbox. Then **Launch nDisplay**.
With Every frame, real-time UE stats appear a few seconds after launch. No stats means the LightAct plugin is not set up correctly.

statements.statement: **Exec cmd line Args**: extra command line arguments (example `-trace` for UnrealInsights). **Custom ExecCmds**: extra console commands.
**Show advanced settings**: **Render offscreen** (no Unreal windows), **Enable mGPU** (render nDisplay viewports on another GPU; needs an NVidia card with NVLink).
**Kill nDisplay** stops the instance. Instances launched by LightAct also die when LightAct exits.
Three workflows: **Thrower2UCam** (most common), **Projector2UCam** (specific cases), **ViewportUCam** (the only one not launching nDisplay from LightAct).
For cases where Unreal's camera is independent of the projectors: cyclo walls, flat or curved walls, domes. A LightAct 3D model gets its content from one thrower.
Create an nDisplay viewport from the thrower in UnrealLink. In Devices create a **Texture Share** device node with the thrower's viewport handle (handles are offered as suggestions). Tick **Listen**.
Route the texture to the thrower through **Render to Canvas**, or directly with **Set Texture**.
For when each projector needs its own point of view (complex 3D objects). The object must also exist in Unreal with the content applied there.
Calibrate projectors in LightAct, generate the .ndisplay from them (one Unreal viewport per projector), launch, read each with a **Texture Share** node, apply to LightAct Projectors in Layer Layouts.
The LightAct 3D model is used only for calibration.
Heavy: one Unreal render per projector. The Unreal scene must match reality: real objects only, matching level of detail, no view-dependent lighting, usually no particles.
Written for UE 4.27. For 5.1.1 or above, contact support.
Texture Share plugin actors: **BP_TextureShare** and **BP_TextureShare_CustomData** (enable **Show Plugin Content** to see them). Put BP_TextureShare in the level. On Play it streams the viewport.
Its **Share Name** variable is the handle. Type the same value as the viewport name in LightAct.
Wrong texture: Unreal cameras must match LightAct throwers or projectors. A **Player start** actor can move the whole nDisplay configuration.
nDisplay fails to launch or crashes: remove all spaces from file paths (above all the .ndisplay path), check nDisplay plugin enabled, check UE and plugin versions, try Unreal's Switchboard.
Written with UE 5.1.1 and LightAct 4.2.2. Most common fault: a space in the .ndisplay path.
Unreal: new project from the **nDisplay template**, copy the plugin into Plugins, enable it.

LightAct, in order: drag the .uproject into a blank project (shows in Assets). Set the UE version in Project Settings. Set UE editor paths in Preferences. Insert one Thrower with nDisplay ticked. In UnrealLink select the .uproject. Click **Generate config file** twice so the file is really written. Show advanced settings, untick **Render offscreen**, Generate command. Launch nDisplay.
Expected: a 1920x1080 px window opens on the primary screen after a few seconds. If not, launch the project with the NDC_Basic configuration from Switchboard.
Then: Devices, insert **Texture Share**, click **LAThrow_0** under Object suggestions to fill **Viewport name**, tick **Listen**.
Support wants: .la project file, .ndisplay file, software versions, GPU and CPU details.

statements.statement: LA4-7358 [B1]: layer crossfade controls removed. Crossfades are configured on sections.

LA4-7357, LA4-6920 [B1]: two defaults. Project Settings holds the project-wide default crossfade and duration, used only for newly created timelines. Timeline Properties holds a timeline default, used only for newly created sections on that timeline. Neither changes existing timelines or sections.

statements.statement: LA4-7386 [RC1]: duration is set directly in seconds; 0 disables the crossfade. "Hold opacity" option keeps the previous FadeHold behaviour.

LA4-7450 [RC1]: "Pause" renamed "Hold" ("Play & Pause" is now "Play & Hold").

LA4-7449 [RC1]: video mode "Freerun & Restart" renamed "Freerun on Hold". Video keeps playing when the playhead reaches the end of a section and holds; a manual pause stops it. statements.statement: LightAct uses dockable windows saved into Workspaces.
Dashboard -> Top Bar (where all windows can be reached).

Track Editor -> Timeline. In LightAct a Track is a lane inside a Timeline where layers are placed. A Timeline has one or more tracks. A project can have several Timelines, managed in the Timelines window.
Layers in LightAct are not strictly defined and are fully customisable.

Devices: in LightAct devices are nodes in the Devices window. They cover Network devices, Trackers, MIDI, Content I/O and Audio devices, for both receiving and sending.
DMX is the exception: there is no DMX device node. Use the dedicated DMX In and DMX Out windows.
Transport: timecode (such as LTC or MIDI) is received in the Devices window.

Since LightAct 4.8, layers can be mapped: directly to viewport objects such as video screens; to canvases (similar to Disguise Feed Maps); to throwers (similar to Disguise Mappings such as Perspective or Spherical).
Fast workflow: most mappings are made by dragging an arrow from the viewport object or canvas to a layer.
Direct mapping: a Layer can map to any Viewport object, any Canvas or a Device.
Perspective mapping -> Perspective Thrower.
Sphere mapping -> Spherical Thrower.
Cubic mapping is also possible -> Cubic Thrower.
Parallel mapping -> Orthogonal thrower.
Layers sit in Timeline tracks. All layers, including stock templates, are built from nodes and can be customised, but normal use only needs the layer variables.
Art-Net or sACN control of a layer variable: click the variable's DMX icon. Incoming DMX data is set and viewed in the DMX In window.
OSC control of a layer variable: click the variable's OSC icon. First set up an OSC Receiver device node, then map values to Layer variables in the OSC In window.

Video assets are normally played with the **Video** or **Multi-layer** stock layer templates. Both contain a **Play video** node, which does the actual playback. The node's inputs match the layer's exposed Layer variables.
Three framerates: **Content framerate** (of the Video asset), **Project framerate**, **Application framerate**.

statements.statement: Purpose: in LightNet, Primary and Editor servers show all content in the Viewport without the cost of full-resolution playback.
Naming: a Video asset with **`_proxyN`** or **`_prxN`** in its name is a proxy downscaled by a factor of N. The Play Video node upscales it by N before passing the frame on.
Example: original `LightAct_showreel_published.mov`, with one proxy downscaled by 2 and one by 4.
Proxy status is shown in the asset's Properties.
A server that should play a proxy always picks the most downscaled one. With `_proxy2` and `_proxy4` both present, it plays `_proxy4`.
Which server plays the original, a proxy or nothing is decided by the Run on logic (lightnet digest, Server workload distribution).
Servers in Base Configuration: a single GPU.

Start in the **Performance** window, **Video playback** section.
**Missed frames** rising continuously: Play Video nodes cannot read, decode and render fast enough. Usual causes: insufficient disk read speed, or insufficient CPU speed.
Missed frames not rising but output still stutters: the cause is something else.

Disk read speed: most likely with large-file codecs (HAP, NotchLC, image sequences). If Decode times and Decompress times are low and frames are still missed, suspect the disk. The Performance window shows current **Disk read speed**.
Background software that uses disk bandwidth (the page names Google Drive) should be disabled on the server.
Decode speed: every codec uses some CPU, including HAP and NotchLC. H.264 needs far more. High Decode and Decompress times in the Play video node graphs point to the CPU.
Framerate: if the video file's framerate is higher than the application's current framerate, frames are missed. The only fix is to raise the application framerate.
Blinking or flickering on videos with an alpha channel: disable the **Frame blending** boolean. With it enabled, semi-transparent pixels may flicker.
